title: Opinions, news and debate
objectives: I can explain why the accents and unusual letters in this unit's words are written and pronounced as they are, using the rules of stress, nasal vowels and letter position.
I can state and defend an opinion with expressions such as na minha opinião and pra mim, and I know what each one says word for word.
I can agree and disagree politely, fully or in part, and soften what I say with expressions like de certa forma and até certo ponto.
I can discuss news and current topics such as education, health, traffic and the environment.
I can report what someone said, asked or requested with disse que, perguntou se and pediu para, and I can explain which parts of the sentence change and why.
I can decide between the indicative and the subjunctive in an argument by asking whether I stand behind the statement.

vocabulary.note: Imprensa means the press as an institution, all the newspapers, television and websites taken together, so it also covers what English calls the media. The m and the n each end a syllable before a consonant, so they only nasalize the vowel: im-PREN-sa is [ĩˈprẽsɐ]. The stress is on the second to last syllable, which is the default for a word ending in a, so no accent is written.

example.target: A imprensa acompanhou o caso durante semanas.
example.source: The press followed the case for weeks.

vocabulary.note: A reportagem is a longer, researched report or feature; a single short item of news is a notícia. The g before e is [ʒ], the s of measure. The word ends in em, which is stressed on the second to last syllable by default (re-por-TA-gem), so no accent is needed. The final em is said [ẽj̃].

example.target: A reportagem mostrou o problema do trânsito na cidade.
example.source: The report showed the traffic problem in the city.
example.source_literal: The report showed the problem of-the traffic in-the city.

vocabulary.note: Tele comes from a Greek word for far, as in telephone, and jornal means newspaper and also a news program. The l at the end of a syllable is said [w], so the word ends like te-le-jor-NAW, and the j is [ʒ]. The stress is on the last syllable, the default for a word ending in l, so no accent. The verb assistir takes the preposition a when it means to watch, which is why you see assistem ao, from a + o.

example.target: Meus pais assistem ao telejornal toda noite.
example.source: My parents watch the TV news every night.
example.source_literal: My parents attend-to-the tele-newspaper all night.

vocabulary.note: Nouns ending in -ista have one form for both genders and only the article changes: o jornalista, a jornalista. Compare o repórter and a repórter. The accent in Brasília follows the rule for words ending in ia (Bra-SÍ-li-a), explained in the spelling note.

example.target: A jornalista entrevistou o ministro em Brasília.
example.source: The journalist interviewed the minister in Brasília.

vocabulary.note: Notícia is one piece of news. English news has no plural, but Portuguese counts them: uma notícia, duas notícias. The adjective falsa follows the noun and agrees with it. Many people say fake news with the English pronunciation. The accent on notícia is explained in the spelling note: the ending ia counts as an extra syllable, so the stress is third from the end.

example.target: Essa notícia falsa circulou em vários grupos de mensagens.
example.source: That fake news story circulated in several messaging groups.
example.source_literal: That news-item false circulated in several groups of messages.

vocabulary.note: The final unstressed e is said i and the t before it becomes [tʃ], like the ch of cheese: de-BA-tchi. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in e.

example.target: O debate entre os candidatos durou duas horas.
example.source: The debate between the candidates lasted two hours.

vocabulary.note: Trânsito is stressed on the third syllable from the end (TRÂN-si-to), so an accent is required. It is a circumflex because the stressed a is followed by an n in the middle of the word, the usual convention for a stressed a, e or o before m or n. The an is a nasal vowel.

example.target: O trânsito está parado na avenida principal.
example.source: The traffic is stopped on the main avenue.

vocabulary.note: Concordar is followed by com: concordar com alguém, concordar com uma ideia. It is built from con (together) and cord, the Latin root for heart, so agreeing is literally putting hearts together. The on is a nasal vowel [õ], and the stress falls on the last syllable (con-cor-DAR), the default for a word ending in r.

example.target: Concordo com você, mas só em parte.
example.source: I agree with you, but only in part.

vocabulary.note: Discordar is followed by de: discordar de alguém, discordar da decisão (de + a). The prefix dis- reverses concordar. Note the different prepositions: concordar com, discordar de.

example.target: Eu discordo da decisão, mas respeito a sua opinião.
example.source: I disagree with the decision, but I respect your opinion.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third syllable from the end (po-LÊ-mi-co), so an accent is required. The circumflex shows a closed e, written because the e is followed by an m: the same pattern as acadêmico. Like all adjectives it agrees: um tema polêmico, uma ideia polêmica.

example.target: A reforma da escola é um assunto polêmico.
example.source: The school reform is a controversial subject.

vocabulary.note: Ser a favor de algo; the opposite is ser contra algo. Favor is a noun, so the phrase literally says at favor, and de links it to what you support. It ends in r, so it is stressed on the last syllable (fa-VOR) with no accent.

example.target: Sou a favor de mais parques na cidade.
example.source: I am in favor of more parks in the city.
example.source_literal: I-am at favor of more parks in-the city.

vocabulary.note: Ser contra algo, with no de. The on is a nasal vowel, and the final unstressed a is the weak [ɐ]: CÕ-trɐ.

example.target: A maioria dos moradores é contra a obra.
example.source: Most of the residents are against the construction.
example.source_literal: The majority of-the residents is against the construction.

vocabulary.note: Pesquisa also means research, and pesquisar means both to research and to look something up online. The u in qui is silent because qu before i is just the spelling of [k]. The first s ends a syllable, and the second s stands between vowels, so it is [z]: pes-KI-za.

example.target: A pesquisa mostra que a maioria quer mais segurança.
example.source: The survey shows that most people want more security.

vocabulary.note: Educação also means upbringing and good manners: falta de educação is rudeness, and mal-educado means rude. English education does not carry that meaning. The ending ão is stressed, so the tilde marks both the nasal sound and the stress, and the ç before a is [s].

example.target: A educação é o tema mais discutido nesta eleição.
example.source: Education is the most discussed topic in this election.

vocabulary.note: Sa-Ú-de has three syllables. The u is stressed and stands next to the vowel a, but it is not part of a diphthong, so it is written ú: this accent keeps a and u from being read as the diphthong au. Saúde! is also what you say when you toast, like cheers.

example.target: A saúde pública precisa de mais investimento.
example.source: Public health needs more investment.

vocabulary.note: Meio can mean half or middle, but here it means medium, the setting something lives in, and ambiente means surroundings, so together they name the natural surroundings. It is a fixed compound noun. The verb cuidar takes de: cuidar do meio ambiente, de + o.

example.target: Precisamos cuidar melhor do meio ambiente.
example.source: We need to take better care of the environment.
example.source_literal: We-need to-care better of-the middle environment.

vocabulary.note: The ending ão is stressed, so the tilde needs no companion accent. The ç is [s], and ei is a diphthong. The plural is eleições, with ões in place of ão.

example.target: A eleição acontece no primeiro domingo de outubro.
example.source: The election takes place on the first Sunday of October.

vocabulary.note: Na is em + a, a preposition fused with the article a, as in the first lesson on contractions. Portuguese uses the article before a possessive here (a minha opinião), where English has none; em minha opinião, without the article, is also correct. Neutral register, fine in speech and writing. Opinião ends in ão, so the stress is on the last syllable and the tilde marks both nasality and stress.

example.target: Na minha opinião, o debate foi muito bom.
example.source: In my opinion, the debate was very good.
example.source_literal: In-the my opinion, the debate was very good.

vocabulary.note: Pra is the everyday spoken form of para, and mim is the form of eu after a preposition. Informal. It marks a personal judgment or taste. In careful writing, use para mim.

example.target: Pra mim, o preço está alto demais.
example.source: To my mind, the price is too high.
example.source_literal: For me, the price is high too-much.

vocabulary.note: A softener. Certo before a noun means a certain, some particular one: de certa forma, até certo ponto. After a noun it means correct: uma resposta certa. So the position of the adjective changes its meaning.

example.target: De certa forma, ele tem razão.
example.source: In a way, he is right.
example.source_literal: Of certain way, he has reason.

vocabulary.note: A softener, like de certa forma. Até means until or up to, and ponto is a point. It limits how far your agreement goes. The on of ponto is a nasal vowel.

example.target: Até certo ponto, concordo com ela.
example.source: Up to a point, I agree with her.
example.source_literal: Until certain point, I-agree with her.

vocabulary.note: Pelo is por + o, by + the, and menos is less, so the phrase picks the minimum you can still say. It often offers a positive point after bad news. It can also mean at the very least in a demand: Pelo menos peça desculpa.

example.target: Pelo menos ninguém se machucou.
example.source: At least nobody got hurt.

vocabulary.note: A softener for agreement and disagreement: Concordo em parte, discordo em parte. Parte is a part, and the final unstressed e is said i, with the t before it [tʃ]: PAR-tchi.

example.target: Em parte, a culpa é nossa.
example.source: Partly, the fault is ours.
example.source_literal: In part, the fault is ours.

vocabulary.note: Seja is the present subjunctive of ser, so the phrase literally says or may it be. It introduces a restatement in other words. It is fixed: it never changes for person or tense.

example.target: Ou seja, o prazo acabou.
example.source: That is to say, the deadline has passed.

vocabulary.note: Portuguese says have reason where English says be right, in the same way that it says tenho trinta anos for I am thirty. The opposite is estar errado. The plural is têm razão, with a circumflex. In razão the r at the start is the strong [h] and the z between vowels is [z].

example.target: Ela tem razão, o preço está alto.
example.source: She is right, the price is high.
example.source_literal: She has reason, the price is high.

dialogues.title: Cell phones at school?
dialogues.context: Tiago and Rafaela discuss a news story about a school banning cell phones from classrooms.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Rafaela, você viu a notícia? A escola do meu primo vai proibir o celular na sala de aula.
lines.source: Rafaela, did you see the news? My cousin's school is going to ban cell phones in the classroom.
lines.source_literal: Rafaela, you saw the news-item? The school of-the my cousin goes to-prohibit the cell phone in-the room of class.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.target: Vi, sim. Na minha opinião, é uma boa ideia. Os alunos olham a tela o tempo todo.
lines.source: Yes, I did. In my opinion, it's a good idea. Students look at the screen all the time.
lines.source_literal: I-saw, yes. In-the my opinion, is a good idea. The students look-at the screen the time all.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Até certo ponto eu concordo. Mas não acho que proibir tudo seja a solução.
lines.source: Up to a point I agree. But I don't think banning everything is the solution.
lines.source_literal: Until certain point I agree. But not I-find that to-prohibit everything be the solution.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.target: Por quê? Pra mim, sem o celular eles prestam mais atenção.
lines.source: Why? For me, without the phone they pay more attention.
lines.source_literal: For what? For me, without the cell phone they lend more attention.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Tenho a impressão de que o problema é mais complicado. Hoje muita gente usa o celular pra pesquisar e estudar.
lines.source: I get the impression that the problem is more complicated. Nowadays lots of people use their phones to look things up and study.
lines.source_literal: I-have the impression of that the problem is more complicated. Today much people uses the cell phone for to-research and to-study.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.target: Isso é verdade. Mas pelo menos durante a explicação eles poderiam guardar o aparelho, né?
lines.source: That's true. But at least during the explanation they could put the device away, right?
lines.source_literal: That is true. But by-the least during the explanation they could keep the device, isn't-it?

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Nisso eu concordo totalmente. O ideal seria combinar as regras com os alunos.
lines.source: On that I completely agree. The ideal would be to agree on the rules with the students.
lines.source_literal: In-that I agree totally. The ideal would-be to-combine the rules with the students.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.target: Exatamente. Meu professor de história disse que ia propor isso na reunião de pais.
lines.source: Exactly. My history teacher said he was going to propose that at the parents' meeting.
lines.source_literal: Exactly. My teacher of history said that he-was-going to-propose that in-the meeting of parents.

lines.speaker: Tiago
lines.target: Então vamos ver o que a direção vai decidir.
lines.source: Then let's see what the school administration decides.
lines.source_literal: Then we-go to-see what the direction goes to-decide.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.target: Pode ser que eles mudem de ideia depois de ouvir todo mundo.
lines.source: They might change their minds after listening to everyone.
lines.source_literal: Can be that they change of idea after of to-hear all world.

dialogues.title: What the TV news said
dialogues.context: Three friends talk about something they saw on the TV news and how to tell if a story is true.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Mariana, você assistiu ao telejornal ontem?
lines.source: Mariana, did you watch the TV news yesterday?
lines.source_literal: Mariana, you attended-to-the tele-newspaper yesterday?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.target: Assisti. A repórter disse que a prefeitura vai fechar a avenida aos domingos.
lines.source: I did. The reporter said that city hall is going to close the avenue on Sundays.
lines.source_literal: I-watched. The reporter said that the city-hall goes to-close the avenue at-the Sundays.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.target: Mas quem falou isso? Eu li que a proposta ainda não foi aprovada.
lines.source: But who said that? I read that the proposal hasn't been approved yet.
lines.source_literal: But who spoke that? I read that the proposal still not was approved.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.target: Foi o que ela falou. Ela disse que o prefeito confirmou a decisão hoje de manhã.
lines.source: That's what she said. She said that the mayor confirmed the decision this morning.
lines.source_literal: Was the that she spoke. She said that the mayor confirmed the decision today of morning.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Eu desconfio. Semana passada circulou uma notícia falsa dizendo a mesma coisa.
lines.source: I'm suspicious. Last week a fake news story went around saying the same thing.
lines.source_literal: I distrust. Week passed circulated a news-item false saying the same thing.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.target: Pois é. A gente precisa checar a fonte antes de compartilhar, né?
lines.source: Right. We have to check the source before sharing, don't we?
lines.source_literal: Since is. The people needs to-check the source before of to-share, isn't-it?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.target: Com certeza. Ontem minha tia me perguntou se eu vi a mensagem no grupo da família.
lines.source: Definitely. Yesterday my aunt asked me whether I had seen the message in the family group.
lines.source_literal: With certainty. Yesterday my aunt me asked if I saw the message in-the group of-the family.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: E o que você respondeu?
lines.source: And what did you answer?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.target: Falei que não acreditava, e pedi pra ela não repassar.
lines.source: I said I didn't believe it, and I asked her not to forward it.
lines.source_literal: I-spoke that not I-believed, and I-asked for her not to-pass-on.

lines.speaker: Beatriz
lines.target: Fez bem. Pelo menos agora ela vai pensar duas vezes.
lines.source: Good move. At least now she'll think twice.
lines.source_literal: You-did well. By-the least now she goes to-think two times.

dialogues.title: A debate about traffic
dialogues.context: Luciana, Fábio and Sandra discuss a proposal for more bicycle lanes in their city.

lines.speaker: Fábio
lines.target: Vocês viram a proposta de criar mais ciclovias na cidade?
lines.source: Did you see the proposal to create more bicycle lanes in the city?
lines.source_literal: You-all saw the proposal of to-create more cycle-ways in-the city?

lines.speaker: Luciana
lines.target: Vi. Eu sou a favor. O trânsito está cada vez pior, e a bicicleta é uma boa alternativa.
lines.source: I did. I'm in favor. Traffic is getting worse and worse, and the bicycle is a good alternative.
lines.source_literal: I-saw. I am at favor. The traffic is each time worse, and the bicycle is a good alternative.

lines.speaker: Fábio
lines.target: Eu discordo em parte. De certa forma ajuda, mas não acho que resolva o problema sozinha.
lines.source: I partly disagree. In a way it helps, but I don't think it solves the problem on its own.
lines.source_literal: I disagree in part. Of certain way helps, but not I-find that solve the problem alone.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Concordo com o Fábio. Pra mim, o mais importante é melhorar o transporte público.
lines.source: I agree with Fábio. For me, the most important thing is to improve public transport.
lines.source_literal: I-agree with the Fábio. For me, the more important is to-improve the transport public.

lines.speaker: Luciana
lines.target: Mas uma coisa não exclui a outra, né? Dá pra fazer as duas.
lines.source: But one thing doesn't exclude the other, right? You can do both.
lines.source_literal: But one thing not excludes the other, isn't-it? It-gives for to-do the two.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Pode ser, mas o dinheiro é limitado. Se gastarem com ciclovia, falta pra ônibus.
lines.source: Maybe, but money is limited. If they spend on bicycle lanes, there won't be enough for buses.
lines.source_literal: Can be, but the money is limited. If they-spend on cycle-way, lacks for bus.

lines.speaker: Fábio
lines.target: Tenho a impressão de que falta planejamento, mais do que dinheiro.
lines.source: I get the impression that it's planning that's lacking, more than money.
lines.source_literal: I-have the impression of that lacks planning, more than money.

lines.speaker: Luciana
lines.target: Nisso vocês têm razão. Pelo menos a discussão está acontecendo.
lines.source: You're right about that. At least the discussion is happening.
lines.source_literal: In-that you-all have reason. By-the least the discussion is happening.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Verdade. E talvez a prefeitura faça uma consulta pública.
lines.source: True. And maybe city hall will hold a public consultation.

lines.speaker: Fábio
lines.target: Tomara. Eu votaria a favor de ouvir a população primeiro.
lines.source: Let's hope so. I would vote in favor of listening to the population first.
lines.source_literal: Would-that. I would-vote at favor of to-hear the population first.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why the accents in this unit's words are written
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is new. Every accent follows the stress rule from the lesson on accents, and every unusual letter follows a sound rule from the lesson on sounds. This note applies those rules to the words of this unit, because an accent you cannot explain is an accent you will forget. The method never changes. Divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default stress from the word's ending, and compare. If the stress agrees with the default, no accent is written. If it disagrees, the stressed vowel carries one: acute if the vowel is open (or alone in a hiatus), circumflex if it is closed.

The largest group is words stressed on the third syllable from the end. No ending predicts that, so an accent is always required. Words that end in ia or io belong here, because the spelling rule counts the i as a syllable of its own even though speech often runs the two vowels together: no-TÍ-ci-a, his-TÓ-ri-a, po-LÍ-ti-ca, Bra-SÍ-li-a, FÁ-bi-o, RÁ-di-o, VÁ-ri-os. Compare ciclovia and geografia. There the stressed vowel is the i itself (ci-clo-VI-a), so the stress is second to last, which is the default for a word ending in a, and nothing is written, exactly as in tia. The same third-from-the-end rule produces polêmico, trânsito, público and ônibus. The choice of mark follows the vowel. An acute on a, e or o means open, and on i or u it only marks the stress. A circumflex means closed, and it is the convention for a stressed a, e or o followed by an m or n in the middle of a word: polêmico, trânsito, ônibus. In words that end in em or ens the acute is written instead, although that e is not an open sound: ninguém, também, parabéns.

Next come words stressed on the second to last syllable whose ending expects the last. Words ending in l, r, z, x, n, i, u or ão default to last-syllable stress, so útil, possível, difícil and repórter break their default and take an accent, acute here because the vowels are open or the i and u have only one quality. The reverse case is words stressed on the last syllable whose ending expects the second to last: você, ninguém and também end in e or em, so they need the accent. Words in -ão and -ões are different, because the last syllable is already the default for ão. The tilde marks the nasal sound and, with no other accent in the word, the stress as well: opinião, educação, eleição, decisão, razão, reunião, população, and in the plural opiniões, eleições.

One-syllable words follow their own rule. A stressed monosyllable ending in a, e or o, with or without s, takes an accent, which also separates it from an unstressed small word: dá (gives) from da (of the), and quê (what, stressed, as in Por quê?) from que (that). The plural têm has a circumflex to separate it from the singular tem, as the lesson on ter showed. Finally, a stressed i or u after another vowel forms a hiatus, meaning two vowels in separate syllables, and is written í or ú when it is alone in its syllable or followed only by s: sa-Ú-de, pa-ÍS. If an r, l, m, n or z closes the same syllable, the consonant already prevents a diphthong reading and no accent is written: pro-i-BIR. The word ideia has no accent because its stress is the default. Before the 2009 spelling agreement it was written idéia, to show the open ei, and the pronunciation [iˈdɛjɐ] did not change.

rows: notícia, história, política, Brasília, família, necessária, Lúcia, Fábio, rádio, vários
The ending ia or io counts as two syllables, so the stress is third from the end and an accent is required.
The stressed vowel is the i itself, so the stress is second to last, the default for a. No accent, like tia.
Third from the end, so an accent; circumflex because the stressed vowel is followed by m or n.
Third from the end, so an accent; acute because u has one quality.
Ending in l or r, the default is the last syllable, but the stress is second to last, so an accent.
Ending in e or em, the default is second to last, but the stress is last, so an accent.
opinião, educação, eleição, decisão, razão, reunião, população, atenção, solução, questão, estão, poderão
The ending ão is stressed by default, so the tilde marks both the nasal sound and the stress.
dá, né, quê, é, já, só
A stressed monosyllable in a, e, o takes an accent; it separates dá from da and quê from que.
The circumflex marks the plural of ter and separates têm (they have) from tem (he has).
The stressed u is in a hiatus and alone in its syllable, so it is written ú.
The stressed i is in a hiatus, but r closes its syllable, so no accent is needed.
The stress is already the default. The acute of idéia was dropped in 2009; the ei is still said open.

examples.source: The report on public health was controversial.

examples.target: Ninguém leu a notícia sobre o trânsito.
examples.source: Nobody read the news item about the traffic.

examples.target: É possível que a opinião deles mude.
examples.source: It is possible that their opinion will change.
examples.source_literal: Is possible that the opinion of-them change.

examples.source: She is right, but they have a different opinion.
examples.source_literal: She has reason, but they have other opinion.

examples.target: O repórter falou da educação e do meio ambiente.
examples.source: The reporter spoke about education and the environment.
examples.source_literal: The reporter spoke of-the education and of-the middle environment.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: nasal vowels, digraphs and the letters that depend on their neighbors
grammar.explanation:
This note covers the letters whose sound depends on their neighbors, in the words of this unit. The principle is the one from the lesson on sounds: Portuguese spelling is a code in which the next letter, or the position in the word, decides how a letter is said. You do not memorize each word. You read the neighbors.

Nasal vowels first. An m or n after a vowel and before another consonant, or at the end of a word, does not make a consonant sound. It only nasalizes the vowel before it. So imprensa is im-PREN-sa [ĩˈprẽsɐ], concordar is con-cor-DAR, and ponto, contra, assunto, tempo and importante work the same way. At the end of a word, em is [ẽj̃], as in reportagem and também, and its plural is ens: mensagens. The endings ão, ões and ãe are nasal diphthongs written with a tilde: educação, eleições.

Letters that change with the next vowel. G is [ʒ], the s of measure, before e or i: reportagem, mensagens, gente, geografia. Portuguese spells the hard sound before e or i with gu, and the u is silent: ninguém. The same design gives qu before e or i, which is [k] with a silent u: que, quem, pesquisa. Before a or o the u is pronounced: quando. The c is [s] before e or i (notícia, decisão, ciclovia), and to get [s] before a, o or u the spelling uses ç: educação, eleição, segurança.

The letters s and x. A single s between vowels is [z]: the second s of pesquisa, decisão, Brasília. The spelling ss exists to write [s] between vowels: assunto, impressão, discussão, assistem. At the end of a syllable, s is [s] in São Paulo and [ʃ], like sh, in Rio de Janeiro: the first s of pesquisa, discutido. The x in the prefix ex before a vowel is [z]: exemplo, exatamente. Before a consonant it is [s]: explicou, exclui. Between vowels in other words there is no rule.

Digraphs, which are pairs of letters that spell one sound: ch is [ʃ] (checar), lh is [ʎ], like the lli of million (aparelho, filhos, melhor), and nh is [ɲ], like the ny of canyon (minha, manhã, tenho). H on its own is silent: história, hoje. Three position rules finish the picture. The l at the end of a syllable is [w]: jornal, telejornal, falta, ideal. In most of Brazil the t and d before the sound [i], an i or a weak final e, are [tʃ] and [dʒ]: debate, notícia, verdade, diretor, gente. And the final unstressed a, e, o are the weak [ɐ], [i], [u]: debate is [deˈbatʃi], governo ends in u. An r at the start of a word is the strong [h] (repórter, razão, reunião), and an r between vowels is a quick tap.

grammar.title: Giving opinions, agreeing and disagreeing
grammar.explanation:
An opinion is a judgment that belongs to the speaker, and stating one involves two separate decisions: whose judgment it is, and how firmly you hold it. Portuguese handles the first with a frame placed before the claim, and the second by choosing the frame and, as the next note shows, by adding softeners. A frame is a short opening phrase that labels what follows as a view and not as a fact. English uses frames too (in my opinion, I think, it seems to me), so the idea is familiar. What differs is the structure of each frame, and the literal column of the table below shows it.

The commonest frame is Eu acho que followed by a clause, a group of words with its own verb. Achar literally means to find, so acho que says I find that, as if the opinion were something you came across. That is why it sounds milder than I am sure, and it takes the indicative, because you are stating what you believe. Na minha opinião is em + a + minha opinião, so it is literally in-the my opinion; the article before the possessive and the contraction na are the ordinary rules. Pra mim is for me, and mim is the form of eu after a preposition. It is the informal choice for personal taste and judgment. Do meu ponto de vista (de + o) is formal and belongs to writing and debates. Tenho a impressão de que is I-have the impression of that: the noun impressão needs the preposition de before que, which English does not need. Me parece que is to-me seems that: parece has no expressed subject, and me says to whom it seems.

To agree, the verb is concordar, which always needs com: concordar com alguém, concordar com uma ideia. English also uses with, but note that Portuguese cannot say concordar alguém. To disagree, the verb is discordar with the preposition de: discordo de você, discordo da decisão. The two prepositions differ, so learn the pairs. Ter razão is to-have reason, the Portuguese way of saying be right, built like tenho fome and tenho trinta anos: Portuguese treats being right as something you have. Nisso eu concordo is in-that I agree: nisso is em + isso, and it points at one specific point, which makes it a way to agree with part of what was said.

Disagreeing follows a social principle. A flat contradiction such as Você está errado attacks the other person, so Brazilians usually acknowledge first and disagree second: Entendo o seu ponto, mas... (I understand your point, but), Pode ser, mas... (literally can be, but), Concordo em parte, mas.... The structure is agree, then but, then your view. The grammar connects to the earlier switch between moods. A positive opinion takes the indicative: Acho que ele tem razão. Negating the opinion verb takes the subjunctive: Não acho que ele tenha razão. Putting the negation inside the clause, Acho que ele não tem razão, keeps the indicative and is a firmer claim, since you are asserting that he is wrong. The version with não acho que only says you do not find him right, which is gentler.

grammar.title: Hedging and softening
grammar.explanation:
A hedge is a word or phrase that lowers how absolute a statement is. Hedges exist because stating an opinion at full strength claims that you are right, and that invites contradiction. Most Portuguese hedges are adverbial phrases. An adverb is a word that says how, how far or how much, and an adverbial phrase is a group of words that does one adverb's job. They stand at the start of the sentence or just before the verb, and they are built from parts you already know: preposition + adjective + noun (de certa forma), preposition + noun (em parte), or preposition + article + word (pelo menos).

Read the parts and the meaning follows. De certa forma is of certain way, and certa means a certain, some particular one. The position of certo decides its meaning: before the noun it means a certain (de certa forma, até certo ponto), and after the noun it means correct (uma resposta certa). Até certo ponto is until certain point, so it draws a limit to your agreement. Em parte is in part. Pelo menos is by-the least, with pelo = por + o and menos meaning less; it names the smallest thing that can still be said, so it is the phrase for the silver lining: Pelo menos ninguém se machucou. De modo geral is of mode general, generally. Na verdade is in-the truth, actually, and it often introduces a correction. Ou seja is or be-it, where seja is the present subjunctive of ser, so the phrase says in other words.

Some softeners act on one word. Meio before an adjective means kind of, and it does not change for gender in this use: Ela está meio cansada, not meia cansada. Meia is the adjective half, as in meia hora. Um pouco is a bit, mais ou menos is more or less, and acho que não is literally I-find that not, a softer no than a bare não. Talvez (maybe) and pode ser que (it may be that) are followed by the subjunctive, because they do not assert anything. English hedges with modals and tag words such as maybe, sort of, I guess. Portuguese adds one more device, the conditional, which you learned for politeness. Eu diria que é caro (I would say that it is expensive) moves the claim away from a bold now.

Softening is not weakness. In Brazilian conversation an argument with a few of these phrases sounds thoughtful and polite, and a sentence without any can sound aggressive. They are especially useful when you disagree with someone older or more senior, and they buy you a second to think.

grammar.title: Reporting what someone said: direct and reported speech
grammar.explanation:
Direct speech quotes the exact words: Ela disse: Estou cansada. Reported speech, also called indirect speech, retells them from the point of view of the person reporting, inside a subordinate clause. A subordinate clause is a clause that depends on a main clause and is attached to it by a linking word; in Ela disse que estava cansada, the main clause is Ela disse and the subordinate clause is que estava cansada. Three things change between direct and reported speech, in English and in Portuguese alike. The linking word depends on the kind of sentence. The person changes, because the point of view moves from the speaker to the reporter. And the tense moves back, because the original moment is now in the past.

The reporting verbs are dizer (disse, the irregular preterite from the past tense lessons), falar, perguntar, pedir, mandar and responder. Dizer que is to say that, and falar que is used the same way in speech, although falar literally means to speak. For a statement, the link is que. For a yes or no question, it is se, whether or if: Você quer café? becomes Ela perguntou se eu queria café. The word order stays ordinary, with no auxiliary verb and no inversion, and the sentence ends with a full stop because it is now a statement about a question. For an open question, keep the question word and drop se: Ele perguntou onde eu morava. For a request, use pedir para plus a subject and an infinitive: Ela pediu para eu esperar. The subject stays as eu because it is a different person from the one who asked; this is the pattern of the lesson on the personal infinitive, which adds an ending only for nós, vocês and eles (pediu para vocês esperarem). The alternative is pedir que plus the imperfect subjunctive: Ela pediu que eu esperasse. The verb mandar is stronger, an order: O chefe mandou entregar hoje.

The tense moves back when the statement was true at the time of speaking and the reporter is looking back. The present becomes the imperfect: Estou cansado becomes Ele disse que estava cansado. Vou ligar, which is ir plus infinitive, becomes ia ligar, where ia is the imperfect of ir from the imperfect lesson, or the conditional ligaria. The preterite simply stays in everyday speech: Eu vi a mensagem becomes Ela disse que viu a mensagem, where English would move to had seen. If the statement is still true now, or you are relaying fresh news, the present can stay: Ele disse que está cansado. The reported speech lesson at level B2 studies the full system of shifts.

Words that depend on where and when the speaker stands also shift, because the reporter is standing somewhere else. In Espere aqui, aqui means here where the speaker is, so the report says ali or lá, there. Hoje, amanhã and ontem shift in the same way, to naquele dia, no dia seguinte and no dia anterior. English does exactly the same: here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day.

grammar.title: Indicative or subjunctive in an argument
grammar.explanation:
A mood is the speaker's attitude toward a clause. The indicative presents the clause as a fact the speaker stands behind. The subjunctive presents it as something not asserted: doubted, denied, possible, wished for or merely conceded. Nothing about the content decides the mood. The speaker's commitment does, and the main verb, the expression or the conjunction before the clause is what shows it. This is the switch from the lessons on the subjunctive, and in a debate you use it constantly, so it helps to have one test. Ask: am I putting this clause forward as true? If yes, use the indicative. If I doubt it, deny it, call it possible or concede it, use the subjunctive.

Verbs and phrases of commitment take the indicative: eu acho que, tenho certeza de que, é verdade que, sei que, parece que. Expressions that withhold commitment take the subjunctive: não acho que, duvido que, não é verdade que, é possível que, talvez, pode ser que. Duvidar needs no negation, because doubt already withholds the commitment. English usually hides this switch (I think he is right, I don't think he is right), while Portuguese shows it. Where the negation sits matters: Acho que ele não vem keeps the indicative, because the negation is inside the clause and you still assert something, while Não acho que ele venha negates the thinking itself.

A concession is a statement you grant without letting it count against your conclusion. Embora (although), mesmo que (even if), a menos que (unless) and caso (in case) introduce clauses that are conceded or conditional, so they take the subjunctive even when the fact is true: Embora more longe, ele chega cedo. Compare Ele mora longe, mas chega cedo, where mas asserts the fact and the indicative is used. In a question, the indicative is the normal choice: Você acha que ele tem razão? asks for an opinion and commits you to nothing. A subjunctive in such a question is possible but marks doubt.

When you report an opinion, the mood stays and the tense moves back. Ele achava que o projeto era bom keeps the indicative and uses the imperfect. Ele disse que não achava que o projeto fosse bom keeps the subjunctive, moving from the present subjunctive (seja) to the imperfect subjunctive (fosse), which is the form taught with the conditional sentences.

culture.title: Conversar sobre o quê? O jeito brasileiro de debater
culture.text:
Brazilians like to talk, and opinions are part of daily life: at the bakery, in a taxi, over a long Sunday lunch. Soccer is the classic topic, and politics can be lively too. There is an old saying that política, religião e futebol não se discutem, literally politics, religion and soccer are-not discussed, meaning that you should avoid them. In practice people discuss them all the time. The art is to disagree without becoming aggressive, which is why softening expressions such as de certa forma and até certo ponto are so common. The title of this note ends with o quê, literally the what, with a circumflex because quê is stressed at the end of a question, unlike the unstressed que in the middle of a sentence.

The news comes from television, especially the evening telejornal, from newspapers and websites, and increasingly from messaging apps. In family groups, a message can be forwarded dozens of times before anyone checks it. The term notícia falsa, or fake news, is now part of everyday vocabulary, and many Brazilians ask Isso é verdade? before sharing something. Checking the source is good manners.

In a conversation, direct contradiction is often avoided. Instead of saying Não, you are more likely to hear Pode ser (literally can be), Mais ou menos (more or less), Depende (it depends) or Eu vejo diferente (I-see differently). These phrases signal disagreement without closing the conversation. A learner who says Concordo em parte, mas vejo por outro lado, literally I-agree in part but I-see by other side, will sound natural, polite and persuasive.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct mood?
choices: Eu acho que ele tenha razão.
Não acho que ele tem razão.
Eu duvido que ele tem razão.
Eu acho que ele tem razão.
exercises.explanation: Positive acho que takes the indicative; não acho que and duvido que take the subjunctive.

exercises.prompt_target: Ontem ele disse que ___ cansado, mas hoje já está bem.
answers: estava
exercises.hint_source: Yesterday he said he was tired, but today he is fine.
exercises.explanation: Reported from a past point of view, the present estou becomes the imperfect estava.

exercises.prompt: Ele disse: 'Vou ligar.' Which is the correct report?
choices: Ele disse que vou ligar.
Ele disse se ia ligar.
Ele disse que liga.
Ele disse que ia ligar.
exercises.explanation: The person changes from vou to a third-person verb, and vou + infinitive becomes ia + infinitive, where ia is the imperfect of ir.

answers: se
exercises.hint_source: She asked whether I wanted to take part.
exercises.explanation: A yes or no question is reported with se. An open question keeps its question word instead.

exercises.prompt_target: Ela pediu ___ eu esperar lá fora.
answers: para
pra
exercises.hint_source: She asked me to wait outside.
exercises.explanation: Pedir para plus subject plus infinitive reports a request. The subject eu is a different person from the one who asked.
